# The Sock Museum

Walt had worked the overnight shift at the Suds-N-Go on Fremont for eleven years before he started the museum.

It began with a single sock, a child's, pale yellow with a cartoon duck whose one eye had been worn away by washing. It sat on top of dryer number six for a week. Walt moved it to the folding table, then to the windowsill, then back to the dryer. Nobody claimed it. On the eighth night he found an index card in the drawer under the register, and in careful block letters he wrote:

*DUCK SOCK, LEFT (PROBABLY). Belonged to a child who was learning to dress himself and insisted on doing it without help. Lost during the great hurry of a Tuesday morning. His mother still thinks about it sometimes, for no reason she can name.*

He propped the card against the sock and felt, for the first time in a long while, that he had done something correctly.

---

By the second year there were forty-one exhibits. Walt had cleared a shelf by the vending machine and lined it with a strip of green felt from the craft store. Each sock had its card.

*ARGYLE, MAROON AND GRAY. Worn to a job interview in 1997 and every important occasion after, as a kind of charm. The job did not work out. The charm, its owner maintains, did.*

*BLACK ATHLETIC, NIKE, SIZE 10–13. One of approximately four hundred identical socks owned by a man who bought them in bulk so he would never have to match them. He did not notice this one was gone. This is the saddest card in the museum.*

*WOOL, HAND-KNIT, BLUE WITH A CROOKED HEEL. The knitter was ninety-one. She got the heel wrong on purpose so her grandson would know it was hers.*

Walt didn't know if any of it was true. That wasn't the point. The point was that someone had worn these things, had pulled them on in the cold dark of some ordinary morning, had walked around inside them, and then one day they were simply gone, into the gap between the drum and the door, into the lint, into the vast quiet country where missing things go. Somebody ought to write it down.

---

The regulars got used to it. A nurse named Priya, who came in at 3 a.m. after her shifts, started bringing him socks from the hospital laundry that had lost their mates. A college kid wrote a card of his own once, taped it up without asking, and Walt left it there because it was good:

*STRIPED, RAINBOW. Bought ironically. Worn sincerely.*

Nobody ever claimed a sock. That was the strange part, or maybe it wasn't. Maybe people understood that once something had a card, it belonged to the museum now. It had become a story, and you can't put a story back in your drawer.

---

The girl came in on a February night when the snow had turned the parking lot into a blank page. She was maybe nineteen, with a trash bag of clothes and the particular stillness of someone who has been crying in a car. She loaded two machines, sat down, and stared at nothing.

After a while she got up and wandered to the shelf. Walt watched her read the cards, one by one, down the whole row. It took her twenty minutes. Near the end she laughed once, a short surprised sound, at the Nike card.

Then she went back to her bag and dug through it and came up holding a single sock. Gray, men's, a hole in the toe.

"Can you do one for this?" she asked.

Walt looked at it. "Where's the other one?"

"He took it." She shrugged, badly. "He took everything. That's the only thing of his that's still in my stuff. I don't even know why I brought it. I was going to throw it out."

Walt took the sock carefully, as if it might be warm. He found a fresh card and a pen and sat at the folding table for a long time, while the dryers turned and turned.

Finally he wrote:

*GRAY CREW SOCK, MEN'S, HOLE IN TOE. Left behind by someone who was not careful with things. It was here for a while and then it wasn't needed anymore. Its former owner is fine. She is going to be fine. She did her laundry in a snowstorm, which is exactly the kind of thing a person does when they have decided to keep going.*

He handed it to her. She read it, and her face did something complicated, and she set the card and the sock on the felt herself, at the very end of the row, straightening it twice.

"Thanks," she said.

"It's a museum," Walt said. "That's what it's for."

---

He thinks about that sometimes, what museums are actually for. Not the grand ones with marble stairs, but the idea underneath them: that the lost things deserve a place. That the ordinary objects of ordinary lives, the ones that slipped away without anyone noticing, might still be worth a card and a strip of felt and a moment of someone's attention at three in the morning.

Everything goes missing eventually. The duck socks and the job-interview socks and the crooked heels knitted by hands that are gone now. The people too, in their way. What you can do, Walt figures, is notice. Write it down. Say: this was here. Someone wore it. It mattered, at least a little, at least to someone.

The girl never came back, which Walt chooses to take as a good sign.

The gray sock is still there, at the end of the row. Every so often, when he's wiping down the shelf, he straightens it.

I like an idea: a man who works nights at a 24-hour laundromat, keeps a lost-and-found of single socks, and writes provenance cards for each one — turning the unmatched socks into a quiet meditation on incompleteness. I'll write that, keeping it under 1000 words.
